838b0a355bf05a52: OCTOBER 23 — “One idiot is one idiot. Two idiots are two idiots. Ten thousand idiots are a political party.”
These days, we have to work increasingly hard to verify what we read on the Internet.
A famous name attached to a quotation is no guarantee that the person actually said it.
So, when I came across the quote, I spent a considerable amount of time trying to trace its origins. I could not establish who first said it in precisely these words.
But I liked its rather wicked observation too much to abandon it. So, a clarification before I proceed.
While the quotation is widely attributed to Franz Kafka on the Internet, there is no reliable evidence that he ever wrote or said it.

The closest documented source appears to be Italian journalist and satirist Leo Longanesi, who wrote in a diary entry dated December 15, 1938 that one fool is one fool, two fools are two fools, but ten thousand fools become a historical force.
The entry was subsequently published in 1947. Somewhere along the way, the historical force became a political party, and Kafka acquired a quotation he may never have uttered.
Imagine this, attach a famous writer’s name to an unverified quotation, and it suddenly acquires intellectual authority.
So, should we attach a political party’s name to an otherwise indefensible position, it could also suddenly acquire legitimacy.
Neither becomes more truthful through the association, but the borrowed authority makes people considerably less interested in asking questions.
Which brings me to Malaysian politics.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Election Commission personnel inspect ballot boxes before they are transported to polling centres for the 16th Negeri Sembilan State Election at the Port Dickson District Administration Complex in Port Dickson on July 31, 2026. — Bernama pic
There is something accurate about the quote’s observation of collective political behaviour.
When an individual politician abandons a principle, we call it hypocrisy. When an entire party does the same, it suddenly becomes strategic co-operation or some commitment to political stability.
Apparently, nonsense becomes considerably more respectable when practised collectively.

Consider what Malaysians have witnessed since 2018. Barisan Nasional (BN) lost federal power after more than six decades. Pakatan Harapan (PH) celebrated the victory as a historic democratic breakthrough.
Two years later, the government collapsed through political realignments. By 2022, PH and BN were governing together.
The parties that had spent years explaining why the other side could not be trusted suddenly discovered the virtues of co-operation.
Former enemies became partners, previous accusations became inconvenient memories, and everything was justified in the name of political stability.
One could almost admire the efficiency with which political principles were rearranged.

By 2026, this flexibility has become considerably more sophisticated. BN governs with PH federally, with Perikatan Nasional (PN) in Negeri Sembilan, and has negotiated an electoral arrangement with PAS in Melaka.
Political differences can be profound in one state, negotiable in another, and entirely irrelevant in Putrajaya.
At this juncture, in fact, political parties should consider a disclaimer such as this: Principles and alliances may vary according to constituency and electoral circumstances.
Then there is corruption, the one political issue everyone condemns until the conversation becomes normalised.

In January 2026, prosecutors announced that no further action would be taken concerning the 47 charges previously brought against Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, citing insufficient evidence following further investigations.
The decision does not establish guilt, and due process must be respected. But questions about prosecutorial independence and institutional accountability remain legitimate.
When an Opposition politician faces corruption allegations, politicians and their supporters demand accountability, sometimes even before investigations are completed.
But when someone from their governing coalition faces controversy, they suddenly remind everyone about due process, the presumption of innocence and the need to let institutions do their work.
Of course, those legal principles are essential. What is rather remarkable is how selectively some politicians remember them.

At this juncture, I would hesitate to describe contemporary Malaysian politics as a country of blindly loyal followers. That would be unfair to all voters and would overlook how much political support has changed.
Many Malaysians are increasingly sceptical of political parties. They have watched enough political manoeuvring to know that today’s promises may become tomorrow’s embarrassments.
Some vote because they genuinely believe in a party’s agenda. Others vote because they distrust the alternatives even more.

Some support individual candidates despite reservations about their parties. And there are those who have become so disappointed with the political establishment that they no longer expect much from anyone.

Voting for a party, therefore, does not necessarily mean believing everything its leaders say. Sometimes, it simply means choosing the option one finds least objectionable. This is where Malaysian politics becomes rather absurd.
Political parties continue behaving as though they command unquestioning loyalty, even when voters may be supporting them reluctantly.
A person can criticise a government throughout its term and still vote for it at the next election, not because the government has earned their confidence, but because the alternative seems worse.
Sometimes, I wonder, this is such a convenient situation for politicians. They no longer have to convince voters that they have kept their promises.
They only have to convince enough people that someone else would do a worse job.
And what are voters supposed to do with all those earlier warnings? Apparently, they are often being told, we should just forget them.
Political circumstances have changed, they are told, and mature voters must understand that compromise is necessary.
Compromise is indeed necessary in politics. But surely there should be some distinction between a reasonable compromise and abandoning everything one previously claimed to stand for.
The more troubling development is that Malaysians may be becoming so accustomed to these reversals that they no longer find them particularly surprising.
A politician breaks a promise, a party changes sides, a former enemy becomes a coalition partner, and the response is increasingly predictable: Well, that is politics.
And what a wonderfully useful phrase that has become. That is politics.
Three words that can explain away almost anything without requiring anyone to explain very much at all.
This is precisely why political disappointment can become dangerous.
When voters expect politicians to break their promises, every broken promise becomes less shocking.
When political deals are assumed to be motivated by self-interest, even the most questionable arrangements begin to look ordinary.
Eventually, politicians may no longer need to defend their inconsistencies very convincingly.
They can simply rely on voters being tired of hearing the same explanations. And that is an extraordinary advantage to give those who hold power.
Political parties are entitled to change their positions. Circumstances change, coalition governments require negotiation, and governing is inevitably more complicated than campaigning.
But those changes should come with explanations. If a party once described another as corrupt or unfit to govern, voters are entitled to ask what has changed beyond the opportunity to share power.
If politicians promised institutional reforms before taking office, they should explain what they have delivered and why other commitments remain unfinished.
If they condemned particular practices while in opposition, they should be prepared to explain why those same practices are now acceptable.
These are hardly unreasonable expectations. Yet in Malaysian politics, asking politicians to remember their own promises can sometimes seem more demanding than asking voters to forget them.
As Malaysia approaches another general election, we can expect the familiar speeches about integrity, reform, stability and the dangers posed by political opponents.
There will be new alliances, old accusations and probably a few remarkable reconciliations between politicians who previously insisted they could never work together.
Some of these compromises may be necessary. Some promises may be sincere. But voters should not have to keep forgetting yesterday’s declarations merely to understand today’s political arrangements.
The danger may no longer be that Malaysians believe everything their political leaders tell them.
It may be that many have heard so many promises and witnessed so many reversals that they have stopped expecting politicians to mean what they say.
And that brings us back to the quote. Ten thousand idiots may or may not make a political party. But it does not take ten thousand idiots to keep political hypocrisy alive.
It only takes enough people becoming accustomed to it, until politicians no longer feel compelled to explain their contradictions.
It is especially troubling about a political system in which voters can recognise hypocrisy perfectly well, yet find themselves repeatedly choosing between politicians who practise it.
Sometimes I think that is the cruellest joke of Malaysian politics today.
Politicians no longer need to command our loyalty. They may only need to survive our disappointment, how convenient it is.
* Khoo Ying Hooi, PhD is an associate professor at Universiti Malaya.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
e4a9a74d06bca39b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — The ringgit opened higher today as the greenback weakened after equity prices fell amid heightened concern over artificial intelligence (AI)-related investments.
At 8 am, the ringgit rose to 4.0785/0855 against the greenback from yesterday’s close of 4.0815/0850.
The ringgit opened higher on Friday as the greenback weakened after equity prices fell amid heightened concern over artificial intelligence (AI)- related investment.
At 8 am, the ringgit rose to 4.0785/0855 against the greenback from Thursday’s close of 4.0815/0850.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the concerns stemmed from investors’ doubts over whether further investments in AI-related companies would generate returns in a timely manner.

He also said the possibility of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve (Fed) is diminishing as two- and 10-year US Treasury yields fell by 16 and 17 basis points to 4.64 per cent and 4.95 per cent, respectively.
Mohd Afzanizam added that the US Dollar Index (DXY) eased 0.15 per cent to 101.625 points.

“However, there is growing concern about growth prospects, making the rate hike decision appear to be unrealistic. As such, ringgit would likely maintain its narrow range trade today as market sentiments look defensive,” he told Bernama.
The ringgit traded mostly lower against a basket of major currencies at the opening.

It edged up vis-a-vis the euro to 4.5765/5843 from 4.5790/5830, but eased versus the Japanese yen to 2.6054/6100 from 2.6035/6057 at Thursday’s close and inched down against the British pound to 5.4664/4758 from 5.4659/4706.
Meanwhile, the ringgit performed mixed against its ASEAN peers.

It gained versus the Thai baht to 12.0852/1124 from 12.0973/1120 at yesterday’s close, and rose against the Indonesian rupiah to 225.8/226.3 from 225.9/226.3. The ringgit was flat vis-a-vis the Philippine peso at 6.42/6.43.
The ringgit eased against the Singapore dollar to 3.1941/1998 from 3.1917/1947 at yesterday’s close. — Bernama
59f4378b7c7909b2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — A 69-year-old man was injured in the shoulder after he was allegedly attacked with a knife by a 13-year-old boy at a public toilet in Kanowit, Sarawak, yesterday.
Sinar Harian reported Kanowit district police chief DSP Junical Ujal as saying police received a report of the incident at 3.29pm.
“According to the call, a 13-year-old boy was reported to have injured a man using a knife.
“The victim is now receiving treatment at Kanowit Hospital and is reported to have suffered minor injuries to his left shoulder,” he was quoted as saying in a statement.
Junical said the case is being investigated under Section 324 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons or means.
He said police are conducting a thorough investigation to establish the full cause of the incident and gather related evidence.
He also urged the public not to speculate or spread unverified information about the case, out of respect for the investigation process and the interests of all parties involved.
Earlier, a claim went viral on social media alleging that a toilet attendant had been attacked by a teenage boy with a sharp object at a public toilet in the district.
5a41a33fb078d2b7: KUALA LUMPUR: Zetrix AI Bhd seems to have missed Thursday's deadline to resolve a covenant breach under its RM2 billion sukuk programme.
As of press time, Zetrix AI had not issued any statement on whether it had secured a waiver from sukukholders or reached an agreement with the sukuk trustee.

Without a resolution, the digital services and blockchain group faces potential repayment obligations of RM2.16 billion, comprising RM2 billion in principal and RM164.5 million in future coupon payments.

The breach arose after managing director Wong Thean Soon ceased to be the company's single largest shareholder following a series of forced share sales linked to margin calls on his share-backed financing facilities.

His combined direct and indirect shareholding fell from nearly 30 per cent to 1.895 per cent as at Oct 15, triggering a breach of the sukuk covenant requiring him to remain the company's largest shareholder.
As at the time of writing, Wong had not responded to Business Times for comment.

In its earlier filing with Bursa Malaysia, Zetrix AI said it would seek sukukholders' consent through an extraordinary resolution, including a possible waiver, if the breach remained unresolved by Oct 22.
Without a waiver, a dissolution event could be triggered, allowing the sukuk trustee to accelerate repayment of outstanding amounts.
However, the missed deadline does not in itself confirm that the trustee has demanded immediate repayment or that a payment default has occurred.

The development adds to pressure on the group, which recently withdrew its proposed interim dividend of 0.25 sen a share, citing the need to preserve working capital amid unexpected operational expenses.
Zetrix AI is also facing scrutiny over RM314 million in unremitted collections owed to the Road Transport Department.

MARC Ratings, meanwhile, has downgraded its sukuk rating to BB+IS from AA-IS and maintained a negative outlook, citing deterioration in its financial and liquidity position, governance concerns and heightened covenant risks.
The company's next move, and whether sukukholders will grant a waiver, remain key uncertainties for investors.
fffe76b7fd765609: TOKYO: Japan's core consumer inflation exceeded the central bank's two per cent target in September for the first time in nine months, data showed on Friday, a sign of broadening price pressure that cements the case for a near-term interest rate hike.

The figures underscored how higher fuel costs from the prolonged Middle East conflict, elevated import prices driven by the weak yen and price pressures from robust artificial intelligence demand were blunting the impact of government fuel subsidies.

Having just raised interest rates last month, the Bank of Japan (BoJ) is set to stand pat on policy next week but may revise up its inflation forecast and signal its readiness to keep pushing up still-low borrowing costs, sources have told Reuters.
"Core inflation is expected to accelerate due to rising energy costs from the Middle East conflict and subsequent second-round effects," said Masato Koike, a senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus.
"But with price rises not accelerating sharply, there's little need for a back-to-back rate increase in October," he said, projecting the BoJ's next hike to come in December.

The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile fresh food but includes fuel costs, rose 2.1 per cent in September from a year earlier, data showed, matching a median market forecast and accelerating from a 1.7 per cent rise in August.

An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BoJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.4 per cent in September from a year earlier after increasing 1.9 per cent in August.
In a sign of broadening inflationary pressure, goods prices rose 2.8 per cent year-on-year in September, accelerating from a 2.6 per cent gain in August, the data showed.
Services inflation also accelerated to 1.5 per cent in September from 1.2 per cent in the previous month, suggesting firms were passing on higher labour costs from a tight job market.
The data will be among factors the BoJ will scrutinise in producing fresh quarterly growth and price forecasts at next week's two-day policy meeting ending on Oct 30.

Sources have told Reuters the BoJ may signal that underlying inflation - or the broad price trend stripping away temporary, one-off factors - likely achieved two per cent, and stress its focus on anchoring inflation around the target.
Governor Kazuo Ueda said last week the BoJ won't tolerate any inflation overshoot, signalling resolve to continue raising rates after lifting them to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent last month.
Recent surveys showed few signs past rate hikes were cooling loan demand, suggesting scope for further rate increases and drawing attention to the BoJ's assessment on lending conditions.
Many analysts polled by Reuters expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 1.50 per cent in December, and predict the terminal rate to be around 1.75 per cent or two per cent.
Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, projects the oJ to leave policy steady next week but signal continued concerns about upside risks to inflation.
"With little evidence that the tightening delivered so far has slowed the economy, the risks are shifting towards a higher peak in the policy rate than our forecast of two per cent," Thieliant said.
170260b06f801d65: BALIK PULAU: Eight Thai citizens were arrested for allegedly operating tomyam eateries using social visit passes and border passes during an integrated operation in Balik Pulau.

The operation was conducted by the Penang Immigration Department in collaboration with the Penang Island City Council, the Companies Commission of Malaysia, and the Department of Labour following public complaints.
Penang Immigration director Syamsul Fitry Ahmad said the operation, which ended at 1am, targeted foreign-run businesses, particularly those operated by Thais.
"Checks led to the arrest of five men and three women, aged between 30 and 40, suspected of running businesses without valid passes or permits.
"Some of them were using social visit passes and border passes," he said.
The eight will be taken to the Jawi Immigration Depot for further investigation and action.
During the same operation, the local council seized all equipment from two premises.
Syamsul Fitry reminded business operators, particularly tomyam restaurant owners, to comply with procedures governing business operations and foreign worker recruitment.
"We have a special pass for tomyam business operators. Employers must ensure that the recruitment of workers complies with all established procedures," he said.
20856c16b40a3284: SEREMBAN: Negri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim has denied reports that he will resign soon to make way for someone else amid the ongoing constitutional crisis in the state.
Ismail, who is also the Juasseh assemblyman, described the claim circulating on social media as merely "political games" by certain quarters.
"Just political games... It is not true. I am not resigning," he said briefly when contacted this morning.
Earlier, a Chinese-language portal reported that Ismail would sign a letter of resignation.
The report, headlined "Ismail Lasim has signed his resignation letter", also highlighted the ongoing administrative crisis involving the palace, which has yet to show signs of being resolved.
Ismail's press secretary, Mohd Fasha Musthafa, also denied the report, describing it as untrue.
"The menteri besar is carrying out his duties as usual. The report (claim) is untrue," he said.
Yesterday, Negri Sembilan Umno liaison committee chairman Datuk Seri Jalaluddin Alias called on all parties to give the state leadership room to resolve the matter.
The former senior executive councillor under the Pakatan Harapan administration said there was no need for concern as the crisis was expected to be resolved soon.
On Sept 20, Istana Seri Menanti announced that the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, had revoked the appointments of 10 executive councillors appointed by Ismail.
The development came after Ismail was reported to have signed a proclamation seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz from the throne on Aug 3, a day after he was sworn in as Menteri Besar.
Ismail also came under the spotlight after Tuanku Muhriz openly reprimanded him following Friday prayers at Masjid Kampung Beting, Juasseh, Kuala Pilah, last week.

b6b00a99b2799e5a: MELAKA: For longtime Duyong resident Aunty Elen, decades of friendship with neighbours of different races have grown into close bonds built on shared experiences, trust and mutual support.
Duyong assemblyman Mohd Noor Helmy shared her story in a video posted on social media.
In the video, Aunty Elen recalls fond memories with her friends, from sharing meals and secrets to making up after disagreements.
"I have been here for a long time. I moved here when I got married 50 years ago," she said, recounting her years in the area.
She spoke warmly of the close ties she shared with her friends, who stood by one another through the ups and downs of everyday life.
"We can argue, but after that, we make up. Sometimes she cries for me, and I cry for her," she said.
Noor Helmy said he had known Aunty Elen as a longtime resident in his constituency and had visited her home after a flood to help resolve a drainage issue.
He added that he often saw her spending time with other residents whenever he visited the area.
He said he shared her story as an example of the close bonds that could develop between people of different races.
"Today, we acknowledge that Malays, Chinese and Indians have no problem being friends. But a deeper bond, a friendship like that between siblings, is something we rarely see," he said.
He said community ties could be strengthened through neighbourhood interactions, business dealings and shared interests.
Neighbours, he added, were often among the first to offer help when someone faced difficulties.

77402c2d0fe4505f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — As you’re reading this, a crowd of Malaysians are triumphantly taking home iPhone Duos much like hunters after a successful foray into the woods.
If you’re perplexed at the reception of this new device from Apple, you are part of a very large non-exclusive club.
So that you don’t have to spend thousands of ringgit without knowing more than “this is Apple’s latest shiny object” I’ll give you a quick lowdown.
What do you mean another iPhone?
Yes, it is a bit confusing that Apple instead of announcing its iPhone line-up in one shot and having them available on the same date, they’ve flipped the script.
This year only the iPhone 18 Pro line and the iPhone Duo, a foldable, were announced in September while being launched on different dates.
The iPhone Duo becomes officially available worldwide in many countries (including Malaysia) today.
Is it really just two iPhones glued together?
No, Apple announced a proper foldable phone though, yes, the duct-taped iPhones meme is very funny.

There is a proper hinge that folds a single display that folds down the centre, with a very nice matte screen — a custom nano-texture finish that apparently minimises the look of the crease, making it nearly invisible in some contexts.

Interestingly the matte finish is replaceable — once the crease gets too worn, you could actually get it replaced but the finish is not the same as the glass beneath, that’s another component that you should try not to damage.
How’s it feel in the hand?
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
It’s a new form factor for Apple that has its quirks and could be an acquired taste. — Picture by Erna Mahyuni
I wasn’t prepared for it to feel so small when folded. Some have compared it to a passport but it feels more like a pocket notebook.
Opened up and laid flat it becomes tablet-like, flat and with a near-indiscernible crease, which is fairly remarkable.
You can also prop it up laptop-style to send emails or watch YouTube videos in a more pleasing manner than even the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max’s display manages.
Yet it is slightly heavier than that phone, which you may or may not consider an acceptable trade-off for productivity’s sake.
Do apps really look funny?
Yes, many apps aren’t as yet optimised for the iPhone Duo. Some work better on the front display instead of on the inner, larger display.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The hinge is fairly solid and the crease not distracting, interestingly enough. — Picture by Erna Mahyuni
Contrary to what many other reviewers are saying, this isn’t actually surprising.
I remember when the iPhone X first launched it still took time for developers and the app ecosystem to catch up to the new touch interface.
Yes, I’m that old.
Old enough to remember some apps looking off dimension-wise or being buggy.
It’s growing pains or first-gen device tax, which is why the advice is usually not to buy them as they’re usually the “devices which Apple use to have us figure out what needs to be fixed.”
Would I like my TNG app to display better on the iPhone Duo? Yes.
Does it bother me that it hasn’t been optimised yet? Not really as the device’s burgeoning popularity is going to be incentive enough for many developers to get with the program.
Something I wasn’t expecting was the sound quality of the iPhone Duo speakers. That doesn’t mean I won’t judge you for playing videos on it in public, though.
Should I go get one as soon as they’re easier to get?
It’s only been a day and trying to figure out how to take pictures, browse the Web, carry it around and do things with and on it has been a bit of a learning curve.
This has to be the first iPhone where I was slightly confused about how to turn it on and getting used to TouchID again after years of FaceID is jarring.
The real test is going to be if I can stick with the phone or run back to the iPhone 18 Pro Max.
Camera-wise, there’s no denying the Pro models have the better camera and if you use the telephoto function a lot (I sure do) you might find the max 2x telephoto limiting.

There is an undeniable charm to the display and if you also love the functionality of the iPad mini, this might be a nice combo of phone and tablet, though realistically more expensive than buying both devices separately.

Check back in a week or two to see if I still like this phone. In the meantime, you can visit the nearest Apple retailer to open and close the iPhone Duo to your heart’s content (or till the retail crew call the cops).

The iPhone Duo is officially available on sale from October 23, but stocks are currently very limited, starting from RM9,499 for the 256GB version, with your colour options being Star White and Night Sky (basically white and deep blue/almost black).

d9518006703b456a: BARCELONA: For weeks La Liga leaders Barcelona have been eagerly awaiting Sunday's Clasico as a chance to stretch the gap between themselves and rivals Real Madrid to a massive nine points.

Some turbulence in the final approach to the clash at Camp Nou has complicated the picture for Hansi Flick's Spanish champions, who suffered their first defeat of the season at Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Tuesday.
By contrast Real Madrid have won four consecutive matches, thrashing RB Leipzig on Wednesday, and starting to look, for the first time since Jose Mourinho's arrival this summer, like a team.

Despite that, the equation remains favourable for Flick. With Raphinha fit again and teenage winger Lamine Yamal enjoying a state of grace, Barcelona will be confident of building on their six-point lead over third-placed Madrid.

A Clasico often proves a fork in the road. Last season Madrid won the first meeting against Barcelona but Vinicius Junior's outraged reaction at being substituted pulled apart the fragile seams of Xabi Alonso's new era.

The Basque coach was ousted little over two months later, and his replacement Alvaro Arbeloa was unable to stop Madrid finishing a second straight season without winning a major trophy, while Barca retained the Spanish title at a canter.
On Sunday Brazil international Vinicius is suspended. Even aside from his underwhelming performances, his absence may help Madrid in terms of providing a clearer path for Mourinho.
"Vinicius's four-match suspension was seen within Real Madrid more as a solution than a problem," wrote Spanish daily AS.
Mourinho has largely deployed all of his team's stars when available, despite the difficulty it poses in terms of a cohesive game plan and finding balance between attack and defence.
Record 140 million euro ($157m) signing Yan Diomande offers more defensively and he is starting to hit his stride going forward, meaning the teenager may be Mourinho's choice against Barca.

An alternative would be to add an extra midfielder to try and disrupt Flick's free-flowing Barcelona, a strategy firmly within Mourinho's wheelhouse, although PSG showed Barca are easier to beat by attacking.

69910b9cecfe2ab1: PARIS, Oct 23 — French authorities yesterday imposed bans or restrictions on fresh protests springing up in the wake of demonstrations last weekend that degenerated into the country’s worst street violence in years.

President Emmanuel Macron said after chairing a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials that curfews and other security measures would be imposed, including bans on “groups without legitimacy” holding protests.
“The priority is a return to calm,” he said.
He added that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide “the next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
He blamed “organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the republic” for the worst of the violence, accusing them of “sedition”.

Officials are still reeling from the clashes, widespread looting and vandalism of public buildings that broke out on October 17, on the margins of mass demonstrations of more than half a million people against the surging cost of living.

Macron’s government has admitted police lost control, and candidates jockeying to succeed him in presidential elections in six months’ time argue that authorities are incapable or unwilling to calm the situation.

A Paris protest yesterday organised by students—who had held four weeks of protests before the October 17 rallies—went ahead, with hundreds attending after an emergency court injunction overturned a police ban.
“The authorities are trying to make a distinction between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ protesters,” said a university student leader, Coppelia Moreau.
“What we are seeing is a government that doesn’t want any demonstrations at all. That goes against the right to demonstrate,” she told journalists.
Protests banned
Officials for the Bouche-du-Rhone region covering France’s second-largest city Marseille banned all protests there tomorrow. The region’s prefecture cited “obvious reasons of security”.
Marseille saw some of the worst violence last weekend.
Hours earlier, the authorities had declared a ban on “all protests” in the southeastern city of Lyon on Saturday.
France’s third-biggest city suffered the looting of 200 to 300 shops last weekend and the torching of a tourist office in what its mayor described as hours of “chaos”.
Other cities, including Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon, issued bans on protests in their city centres.
France’s interior ministry said “20 per cent more” police would be deployed tomorrow than for last weekend.

In Paris, the city’s police said that the march planned for tomorrow could be held in the east of the capital, starting at Bastille—but it was banned from heading into the city centre, where shops and major public buildings are located.
Yellow Vest movement activists organising the cost-of-living rallies along with unions said it did not agree with the order.
“We won’t sign off on it,” said Benjamin Ball, who runs an online map showing the planned locations of Saturday’s demonstrations.
Art Basel Paris, the capital’s biggest art fair, said it would shut this weekend, two days early, due to the protests.
The culture ministry announced the closure of several Paris museums, Saturday, including the Louvre and the Orsay museum, which houses 19th-century art including the Impressionists.
Detentions and dialogue
The French government has been projecting a firm response in the wake of last weekend’s violence.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said that 217 people of 2,700 arrested during and since last weekend had already been convicted and jailed, and that 1,000 more were being prosecuted.

On Thursday, a 66-year-old man was arrested over the arson last weekend of the 19th-century town hall of Limoges, prosecutors said. A man in his 30s had already been arrested Tuesday over the same crime.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader currently topping opinion polls for the April-May presidential elections, has accused Macron and his centrist government of being too soft and lacking authority.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a far-left candidate criticised by the government for not strongly condemning the protest violence, blamed authorities’ “non-stop brutal repression” for the unrest.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Thursday hosted a meeting of top officials from France’s main parties. While most sent their leaders, Le Pen’s National Rally was represented by a lower-ranking party official.
On Monday, Lecornu will meet student groups, unions and the employer federation. — AFP

cbb312682a35ae36: PETALING JAYA, Oct 23 — As far as restaurant names go, Human Beings Everybody Noodles takes the cake.
It’s the translated name of Jinrui Mina Menrui, one of Osaka’s most popular ramen restaurants and a 2025 pick for the city’s top 100 ramen shops on Tabelog.
Tabelog is widely regarded as Japan’s most reliable restaurant review platform, famous for a strict, weighted scoring system under which 97 per cent of listed eateries score below 3.5 stars.
Jinrui Mina Menrui holds 3.75, if you’re wondering.
Takahiro Matsumura founded the restaurant in 2012, and it built a large following on housemade wheat noodles and a clean shoyu broth of clams and chicken bones.
That success gave him the foundation to launch a slew of other concepts, including the similarly eccentric The Most Deserted Ramen-Bar in the World and The Old Man’s Best Swing.
Last year, parent group Unchi Co announced a global expansion on its website.
This August, Jinrui Ramen arrived in Malaysia, opening its first location in Damansara Perdana.
To make sure its offerings are available to just about “everybody”, the outlet serves no pork, no lard and no alcohol.
Its website states that all ingredients come from halal-certified suppliers, though the restaurant itself is still pending halal certification.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The restaurant is full of art depicting historical figures like Albert Einstein and P. Ramlee eating ‘ramen’. — Picture by Ethan Lau
I guess pescatarians, vegetarians, and their ascetic branch, vegans, don’t count as “everybody”.
But in keeping with the theme, the space is littered with art depicting everyone from Einstein to P. Ramlee eating ramen.
Ironically, the images strongly resemble AI-generated art. The medium is the message, folks.

Sitting at the counter, I watched a “live” concert by a Japanese pop-rock band on TV. As time went by, I realised everybody in the restaurant was hostage to a never-ending loop of that same band’s concert videos.
But it wasn’t too bad, all things considered. Though I didn’t understand anything, it’s much, much better than being forced to listen to Ed Sheeran.
My always-listening phone later identified them as Mr Children, Matsumura’s favourite band, and a few blogs suggest most Jinrui locations blast them all day long.
The menu is focused: four variations of the broth (Premium, Micro, Macro and Red) and the same four for the dry mazesoba.
The Red is a spicy variant launched just for our Malaysian taste buds, while Micro and Macro are named after compilation albums by, you guessed it, Mr Children.
The calling card is the Premium (RM29): chewy, medium-thick wheat noodles in a clam and chicken shoyu broth layered with scallop oil.
Toppings are kept simple, with sous vide chicken chashu, sliced negi and fresh aka kaiware, red radish sprouts with a distinctly peppery bite.
A soy-marinated egg (RM3) costs extra. There’s a deep sweetness to the clear beige broth, and the clam comes through with real clarity.
It isn’t a salty, fatty, tonkotsu-esque affair, so if that’s what you look for in ramen, stop reading now.
The slick, chewy noodles are the real highlight. Whatever the ratio of soft to chewy is, they’ve found it.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A ‘ringan’, or lighter portion of ‘mazesoba’, Jinrui’s dry offering showcases its chewy noodles very well. — Picture by Ethan Lau
For more thorough enjoyment of the noodles, I opted to try them dry. Thankfully, the mazesoba also comes in a half-portion, which I ordered in the Micro (RM15).
Despite the name, it’s a veritable flavour bomb, powered by the savoury aroma of garlic.
It’s fairly salty, a sensation compounded by the irresistible texture of the noodles, but the saltiness is a little one-dimensional, and I’d struggle to finish a full bowl on my own.

The diminutive cubes of sous vide chicken don’t help. Diced chicken doesn’t cling to tossed noodles, particularly ones with this little oil, and you end up with a pile of rubbery bits at the bottom of the bowl.
The thick slices used for the ramen would have served it better.
It is, however, a real joy to see more regional and specialised ramen arriving in Malaysia.
After the initial wave in the early 2000s, the market settled into a narrow idea of the dish that revolved almost exclusively around tonkotsu.
But over the last few years, the arrival and success of concepts like Enishi and Minamo suggest there is a market for ramen beyond tonkotsu.
Jinrui is the latest to join the field, offering a ramen unlike anything else in our market.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Look for the sign on the ground floor of Neo Damansara. — Picture by Ethan Lau

3dee228e957f9414: KUALA LUMPUR: Surging oil tanker rates amid the Middle East conflict could raise operating costs for Malaysia's oil and gas (O&G) industry, although economists said upstream producers and tanker operators may benefit from higher crude prices and charter rates.

Oil tanker rates for very large crude carriers (VLCC) from the Persian Gulf to Asia climbed to more than US$37 per barrel by mid-October, more than five times their pre-conflict levels, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Wednesday.
The agency attributed the surge to congestion in the Strait of Hormuz, trade rerouting and increased ship-to-ship transfers since the conflict began in late February.
These disruptions have lengthened delivery times and reduced fleet efficiency, pushing freight rates higher.

As of the latest reports available up to Oct 22, VLCC tanker rates on key Middle East-to-Asia routes have reached US$1 million to US$1.4 million a day, although some routes have eased from their peaks.
At a daily equivalent rate of US$1.4 million, a 30-day round voyage would imply about US$42 million in time-charter-equivalent earnings.
Revenue Gains, Cost Pressures
Economists noted that the impact on Malaysia would be mixed, with higher crude prices potentially boosting petroleum revenue and encouraging exploration and production (E&P) activities.
Rising transportation and insurance costs could squeeze refining margins, increase fuel subsidy requirements and raise business operating costs.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said higher fuel and insurance costs were pushing up transportation expenses, requiring O&G companies to strengthen cost management and improve productivity.

"The O&G industry would need to be vigilant in managing their operating costs by ensuring operational excellence as their main tools to manage costs, along with increasing the productivity level," he told Business Times.
Afzanizam said oil transportation costs could rise further if the conflict persisted.
He added that disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz could increase the need for E&P activities as energy security risks remained elevated.
Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the impact of higher freight rates would vary across the O&G value chain.
"The impact is mixed. Higher freight costs will squeeze refining margins and increase crude import costs, while tanker operators such as MISC Bhd could benefit from stronger charter rates.
"Upstream producers should remain relatively insulated," he said.
Thong said further disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with higher insurance premiums and vessel shortages, could push freight rates higher.
However, he noted that rates were already exceptionally high and could retreat sharply if geopolitical tensions eased.
"Higher crude prices should benefit upstream producers and potentially increase government petroleum revenue.
"However, Malaysia is also a net importer of crude oil, meaning higher freight and energy costs could pressure refiners, increase subsidy requirements and raise business operating costs," he said.
Thong said the benefits would therefore be concentrated in upstream production and shipping, while the wider economy faced higher cost pressures.
Transport Cost Spike Seen Temporary
LBB International chief executive officer Dr Marco Tieman expects the impact on Malaysia's transportation costs to be temporary, despite the prospect of further escalation in the Middle East.
"The situation is a little bit fluid with an increasing escalation in the Middle East expected in the coming weeks.
"I don't think this will be long term impact to the transportation costs for Malaysia," he said.
Tieman added that Malaysia is in a favourable position as a significant O&G producer.
Nevertheless, the IEA has noted that the disruption extended beyond crude oil shipments, affecting the availability of vessels used to transport refined petroleum products.

The agency said exceptionally high earnings from crude shipping had encouraged some tanker owners to redeploy Long Range 2 (LR2) vessels, which are commonly used for long-haul oil product shipments, to carry crude instead.
This has reduced vessel availability in the oil product tanker market, pushing up freight rates as cargoes are redistributed among smaller vessels.

By mid-October, freight rates for Long Range 1 (LR1) tankers travelling from the Persian Gulf to Japan had climbed to nearly US$27 per barrel, about five times their pre-conflict levels, the IEA said.

The agency also reported that shipping costs had risen sharply on other routes, with rates for Suezmax tankers carrying crude from West Africa to Europe exceeding US$22 per barrel by mid-October, more than four times their pre-conflict levels.

4d29088ae4209af0: MIAMI, Oct 23 — A US judge yesterday issued President Donald Trump a December 11 deadline to testify under oath in his US$10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16.
If Trump fails to attend the deposition by then, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.

Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary Trump: A Second Chance to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, after losing the presidential election.
The crowd proceeded to storm Congress in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s victory.

While the BBC has apologized for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.
Trump filed his suit against the BBC in December 2025 and is seeking at least US$5 billion on each of two counts.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said in court that Trump had no real excuse not to testify and that on October 16, he had only been campaigning, “participating in party politics.”
“No plaintiff is above the law,” Tobin said.
In a court filing Wednesday, Trump’s legal team argued that he was not seeking to avoid a deposition but had been constrained by “matters of national importance.”
The lawyers said Trump would be able to give a deposition between January 11 and 22.

Trump has made attacks on the media a signature of his two presidential terms, insulting reporters who ask questions he doesn’t like and seeking to ban outlets airing critical reports from the White House.
Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.

With his approval ratings in the low 30 per cent range and polls showing his Republican Party likely to lose control of the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, Trump faces increasing headwinds as he approaches his final years in power. — AFP

cf93b3725f09461b: NEW YORK, Oct 23 — New York’s city council yesterday voted to ban horse-drawn carriages in Central Park, signaling the end of a tourist ritual that’s been subject to years of heated debate.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who must sign the measure into law, had previously voiced support for such a ban but has also expressed concerns regarding protections for workers in the industry.
If the mayor signs it, the ban will go into effect in June of 2028.
The lead-up is meant to help the approximately 150 active carriage drives find new employment, city council speaker Julie Menin told journalists ahead of the vote.
The Transport Workers Union representing those laborers have vowed court action.
Legislative battles over the fate of the cultural tradition that’s nearly as old as Central Park itself have been ongoing for nearly two decades.
Critics say the animals suffer, pointing to deadly collapses and dangerous escapes, while advocates point to the jobs they create and the heritage they uphold.
The bill includes a provision for exploring potential compensation for license holders, Menin said.
It mandates that owners of the nearly 200 horses would not be allowed to sell them for slaughter or for the purposes of other horse-carriage businesses.

The rides—enshrined in film and television including Robert Redford and Jane Fonda’s scene in “Barefoot in the Park,” or a dramatic ride in “Sex and the City”—currently run for US$150 for 45 minutes up to several hundred dollars for a marriage proposal.
But after years of wrangling over the issue this past summer season proved decisive in sounding the death knell for the Manhattan carriages.
This past June a 18-year-old tourist from India was killed by a horse that got loose and bolted.
That followed a series of other incidents with the carriages, including the deaths of several horses.

The Central Park Conservancy, which manages the US’s most frequented urban park with 42 million annual visits, even threw its weight behind the calls for a ban, saying it had become “a matter of public health and safety.” — AFP
e2d751cb90036dab: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 — Construction of a massive arch in Washington proposed by US President Donald Trump could move ahead despite ongoing legal action, with a recent court filing saying work could begin in two weeks.
The proposed giant structure along the Potomac River near Arlington National Cemetery is part of Trump’s drive to put his personal stamp on the US capital.

In a Wednesday court filing, the Trump administration said “construction could commence as early as November 5,” the same day the commission aligned with Trump is set to vote on approving the project’s proposed site and building plans.
The planned 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal white arch—dwarfing the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, its inspiration—would also feature gold statues of an angel and eagles at the top.

The project’s height would interrupt the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial, one of Washington’s iconic landmarks, and Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American servicemembers.

In September, US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the Trump administration “provide the court with 48 hours’ notice before engaging in any activity” on the site “related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch.”
The lawsuit against the project was filed in February by Vietnam War veterans, who argued that such a massive undertaking requires approval by Congress.
Since returning to office in 2025, Trump—a former real estate mogul—has launched a series of renovation projects, several of which have prompted legal disputes.

They include a massive, costly ballroom being built at the White House, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished, and the Kennedy Center performance venue, which the president threatened to demolish unless his name was displayed on it.

The most recent instance of this involves the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic golf course Trump wishes to redesign but has faced legal setbacks after hundreds of trees were cut down for the project. — AFP
8071db183c816bf2: JAKARTA, Oct 23 — Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said on Thursday that the government would revoke the business licences of foreign-owned companies found to have repeatedly violated regulations and contributed to forest and land fires, reported Xinhua.
Prabowo said authorities were investigating companies suspected of violating land management and fire prevention regulations, with preliminary findings indicating repeated violations by some firms.

63af7376d5ba2018: GEORGE TOWN, Oct 23 — The driver suspected of being involved in a hit-and-run accident that killed two people on the Tun Dr Lim Chong Eu Expressway near the Penang Bridge interchange yesterday morning has been arrested.

868cdccf99a4f933: WHY do bosses repeatedly turn to certain members of staff when there is a job to be done?
Why do some employees seem to carry a heavier burden than others, often becoming the first people approached when deadlines loom, problems arise or expectations are not being met?
The answer lies in a combination of trust, competence, reliability and attitude.
In every workplace, there are people who do more than simply fulfil the requirements of their job. They make things happen.
Their value is not always reflected in their job title, salary or position on the organisational chart, but it becomes unmistakable when something important needs to be accomplished.
These employees have earned something that cannot easily be demanded or manufactured: confidence in their ability to deliver.

When a boss assigns a task, there is always an element of risk. Will it be completed on time? Will the quality be acceptable? Will someone need to be constantly reminded, supervised or rescued along the way?

Employees who consistently deliver reduce that uncertainty. A manager can hand them a responsibility and concentrate on other matters, knowing that the work is likely to be completed without unnecessary drama.
Reliability, therefore, is a valuable workplace currency. It is built through repeated actions, not grand promises.
People who keep their word, meet deadlines, communicate honestly and take responsibility for their mistakes gradually become the people others depend on.
Another important quality is the ability to find solutions rather than merely identify problems. Every workplace encounters obstacles, misunderstandings and unexpected setbacks.
Some employees wait for instructions whenever something goes wrong. Others assess the situation, consider the options and suggest a practical way forward.
This does not mean that valuable employees must have every answer. It means they are willing to think, exercise judgement and make a constructive contribution.
They understand that the objective is not simply to explain why something cannot be done, but to explore how it might be achieved.
Initiative also sets these employees apart. They do not always wait to be asked before noticing what needs attention.
They anticipate difficulties, recognise opportunities for improvement and act within the limits of their authority.
Their contribution extends beyond the immediate task because they understand the wider objective.
Equally important is their attitude towards responsibility. When a task becomes difficult, they do not immediately search for someone to blame.

They focus on what can be controlled, acknowledge their part in a problem and work towards a solution. This sense of ownership gives managers confidence that challenges will be addressed rather than quietly abandoned.
Communication is another defining characteristic. Employees who provide clear updates, raise concerns early and ask sensible questions make it easier for others to do their jobs.
They do not leave their managers guessing about progress or conceal problems until it is too late to resolve them. Good communication builds trust because it replaces uncertainty with information.
There is also the question of emotional maturity. Workplaces involve different personalities, competing priorities and occasional tension.
People who remain composed under pressure, accept feedback without becoming defensive and disagree respectfully are often particularly valuable.
They help maintain momentum when circumstances become stressful, rather than adding another problem for everyone else to manage.
These qualities explain why certain employees are repeatedly chosen for important assignments. However, there is a less comfortable side to this pattern. Being dependable can become a burden.
Once a manager discovers who can be trusted to deliver, it is tempting to keep returning to the same person, even when others could reasonably share the responsibility.

What begins as recognition can gradually become overreliance. The capable employee receives more work, more urgent requests and more difficult assignments, while colleagues with less initiative may escape the same level of scrutiny.
Eventually, competence is rewarded with an ever-growing workload rather than greater opportunity, recognition or support.
This is where good management matters. A capable employee should not become the permanent solution to every organisational problem.
Managers must distinguish between recognising someone's strengths and taking unfair advantage of their willingness to help.
Work should be distributed sensibly, expectations should be realistic, and exceptional contributions should be acknowledged.
It is also worth remembering that being repeatedly selected does not always mean an employee is the most talented person in the room.
Sometimes the decision reflects familiarity, convenience or a manager's preference for someone who works in a particular way.
Good leaders must remain alert to favouritism and ensure that quieter employees are not overlooked simply because they promote themselves less confidently.
For employees, the lesson is equally important. Being dependable is a strength, but it should not require unlimited availability or the silent acceptance of unreasonable demands.

The ability to set boundaries, communicate capacity and ask for support is part of professional maturity. Sustainable performance is more valuable than a short burst of extraordinary effort followed by exhaustion.
Ultimately, bosses turn to particular staff members because those employees offer something more meaningful than obedience.
They offer confidence. They combine competence with judgement, responsibility with initiative, and commitment with the ability to work constructively alongside others.
Their greatest value is not that they can be given more work than everyone else.
It is that they make difficult things easier, uncertain situations more manageable and shared objectives more achievable. They are the people who turn intentions into results.
But organisations must recognise a fundamental truth: the people who consistently get things done should not simply be given more to do.
They should be developed, respected, fairly rewarded and given opportunities to grow. Otherwise, the very qualities that make them valuable may eventually become the reasons they leave.

a52a4b92f90e0388: In a matter of just over a month, a perfect storm has pushed Zetrix AI Bhd to the precipice of corporate oblivion. In the process, the digital services firm’s share price has crashed by over 90% and its market capitalisation has plummeted by over RM5 billion.

The collapse of its shares started on Aug 27 when it opened at 66 sen, with the company valued at about RM5.33 billion. By the end of the day, the company formerly known as My EG Services Bhd had fallen nearly 10% to 59.5 sen.
The next day, the dam broke when the shares suffered a intraday plunge of 50.4% to close at 29.5 sen, erasing RM2.4 billion from its market value.

The monumental collapse was attributed to speculation linking it with the corruption case of former human resources minister M Saravanan as well as forced selling of the shares of its co-founder and group managing director Wong Thean Soon.

Things got progressively worse with the share price falling like a rock as the bad news piled up. On Oct 5, the Road Transport Department (JPJ) suspended Zetrix and its subsidiary MyEG Sdn Bhd as collection agents over unremitted government revenue.
Transport minister Loke Siew Fook then dropped the bombshell that Zetrix failed to remit RM314 million in collected government revenues.
This prompted the police to open an investigation into the matter, with the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) also jumping into the fray.
The troubles afflicting Zetrix put it firmly in the crosshairs of rating agencies. On Oct 18, 2026, MARC Ratings downgraded its RM2 billion sukuk (Islamic bonds) programme rating to BB+IS from AA-IS.
The stock then tumbled on news of a potential covenant breach looming over the sukuk programme. Under its trust deed, Wong is required to remain Zetrix’s single largest shareholder.

However, his stake has been slashed to just 1.84% currently from nearly 30% following forced share sales by banks triggered by margin calls. The sukuk trustee has given Zetrix until Oct 22 to remedy the issue, which seems highly unlikely given Wong is no longer a substantial shareholder.

This means it needs to seek sukuk holders’ approval for a waiver if the breach is not resolved by then. Without a waiver, the breach could trigger early repayment of the RM2 billion principal as well as RM164.5 million in future coupon payments.
Any default of the sukuk will trigger a Practice Note 17 (PN17) classification. That would be catastrophic for Zetrix.
To aggravate matters, the company announced it was withdrawing its first interim dividend of 0.25 sen per share (amounting to RM19.7 million) for FY2026 declared two months ago to “conserve cash”.

In the face of all the bad press, Zetrix’s share price hit an intraday low of 5 sen last Friday (Oct 16), its lowest level in over 14 years, valuing the company at RM404 million. The stock is within touching distance of its all-time low price of 3.5 sen, which was reached in 2008.
Zetrix’s paradox
Ironically, Zetrix should be trading nearer to its all-time high than its record low, based on its financial results.
For the year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025), its net profit hit RM883.85 million, a 24.9% rise from the previous year, while revenue jumped 31.3% to RM1.34 billion.
Just two days before Zetrix’s selloff started end-August, MBSB Research forecast it would hit RM1.1 billion in core earnings for FY2026.
MBSB noted Zetrix’s normalised earnings for the first half of 2026 jumped 38.9% to RM540.7 million, and was on track to achieve the RM1 billion earnings milestone.
On the face of it, companies having such strong financial performance should not be trading at 5 sen. That is the paradox facing Zetrix.
Its financials are the not the problem, rather it is a crisis of confidence. For Zetrix, restoring confidence in the company is paramount.

Under Wong’s leadership, the group realised its e-government services business model was inherently risky as the need for such a “middleman” was untenable in the long run. The expansion of the MyJPJ app signals the government is increasingly capable of providing digital services directly.

Its name change last year to Zetrix from My EG is a reflection of its strategy of transforming itself from an e-government services provider into a blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) company.

Its robust financial performance in recent years can be attributed to this transformation. Blockchain and AI-related revenue increased from RM127.6 million in 2023 to RM362.8 million in 2024, and RM643.5 million in 2025.

Its first half FY2026 earnings of over half a billion ringgit was supported by AI subscriptions and services, Web3 application fees and sales of Zetrix Layer-1 nodes. Nevertheless, non-AI and non-blockchain activities still account for about 40% of group revenue.
However, this transformation seems to have become its achilles heels as it has racked up huge debt to roll out the new business.
By end-June 2026, cumulative development expenditure had reached a whopping RM3.7 billion from RM2.85 billion at end-2025. That expenditure is likely to continue growing.

At end-June, Zetrix had RM541.6 million in cash and cash equivalents against RM853.1 million in short-term loans and borrowings. Total borrowings stood at RM2.2 billion, up 74.3% from RM1.26 billion a year earlier.

Its current financial woes may well be linked to the burgeoning debt to finance its investment in blockchain infrastructure, AI applications and international expansion. The question remains whether Zetrix has bitten off more than it can chew?

While the transformation appears to be bearing fruit with rising revenue and earnings, investors and financial institutions want to know if these are recurring and sustainable, given the huge investment involved.
Last throw of the dice

Zetrix may have a trump card to deal with its rising debt and cashflow issues as it is preparing to list its AI and blockchain unit, AI Foundation Lab, on the Nasdaq by end-2026. The plan is even backed by a US$40 million (RM163 million) equity investment from International Finance Corp, the World Bank’s investment arm.

The company is targeting a valuation of US$3 billion (RM12.2 billion) alongside a US$200 million (RM816.3 million) capital-raising exercise before the listing, according to a CLSA note. It plans to eventually pare down its stake in the US-listed company, with proceeds to be used to reduce its debt, and potentially pay a special dividend.

However, these projections were done prior to the brutal selloff, which has thrown a spanner into the works. MARC said its proposed Nasdaq listing could be deferred to the first quarter of 2027 from its initial end-2026 target.
“While the proposed listing could broaden the group’s access to capital, recent developments affecting its business and financial profile could present challenges to its completion,” it said.
It added Zetrix’s reliance on “transactions that remain subject to execution risks” offered limited assurance that funds would be available in time for debt repayment.
This potential Nasdaq listing may well be the last throw of the dice for Wong and Zetrix. If it is executed successfully, they may well be able to prevent the company from falling off the precipice.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
bff2e4ccd2a52b16: PETALING JAYA: Taking the dog for a walk? Don't forget the leash, a bag for the poop - and, apparently, a bottle of water for the pee.
That's the unusual message from Vienna, Austria, where dog owners in one neighbourhood are being encouraged to rinse away their pets' urine to protect trees and other greenery.

The initiative, called "Schönes Gassi", or "nice dog walk", was launched on Oct 12 in Neubau, a densely populated district of the Austrian capital. The voluntary campaign encourages owners to carry small bottles of tap water and pour some over areas where their dogs have urinated.
According to The Guardian, the district is even distributing free 270ml bottles to encourage participation. It's a simple idea that might raise a few eyebrows, but there's a serious reason behind it.

Neubau is home to around 600 dogs, many of which regularly use the same trees and patches of greenery to relieve themselves. While marking territory is perfectly natural canine behaviour, repeated exposure to urine can damage urban trees.

According to the campaign's organisers, chemicals in dog urine can harm tree bark, weakening its protective layer and potentially allowing fungi and other pathogens to enter. Over time, this can lead to decay and compromise a tree's stability.

That's particularly concerning in neighbourhoods where trees provide much-needed shade and help cool surrounding streets. Neubau has planted around 200 trees over the past decade, making their protection an important local priority.

Fortunately, fresh dog urine is highly water-soluble, so rinsing the affected area helps dilute substances that could cause damage or unpleasant odours. Of course, the water bottle isn't a free pass for Fido to pee wherever he pleases, and owners are still encouraged to steer their pets away from vulnerable greenery.
A little consideration goes a long way
Rather than introducing restrictions or penalties, the organisers hope to encourage small changes in behaviour that make shared urban spaces more pleasant for everyone.
Dog trainer Conny Sporrer, who supports the initiative, told reporters that pets can be taught where they should relieve themselves.
"We need neither a city full of dog bans nor a city where dogs can simply pee anywhere," she said, emphasising the importance of consideration, education and suitable facilities.

Similar practices have been adopted in parts of Japan, Spain, Italy and Switzerland, suggesting the idea isn't quite as unusual as it first sounds. Nevertheless, some Vienna dog owners have bemoaned having to carry another item while out on a daily walk.
For now, participation remains entirely voluntary.

The idea might also strike a chord with Malaysian dog owners and their neighbours, given the occasional disputes over pets urinating on pavement flowerbeds, outside residential gates or around the roots of carefully tended trees.

For residents who take pride in their gardens, repeatedly finding that a passing dog has left its mark can understandably be frustrating. Encouraging owners to carry a small water bottle could help reduce unpleasant smells while showing consideration for others.

Naturally, prevention is preferable to rinsing afterwards, and keeping dogs away from neighbours' plants should remain the priority. But perhaps there's something worth borrowing from Vienna's approach: responsible pet ownership needn't always involve complicated rules or expensive solutions.
Sometimes, a little water and a little thoughtfulness might be all it takes to make neighbourhood life more harmonious.
8cc752ce01a6e530: PETALING JAYA: Ketabahan membawa Mohammad Fitri Aziz keluar daripada belenggu psikotik yang sukar kepada menjalani kehidupan yang teratur dan stabil, selepas bertahun-tahun hidup dengan skizofrenia.

Dahulu Fitri, 31, lebih berusaha untuk sembuh sejak didiagnosis pada 2020, tetapi kemudian beliau belajar memahami diri sendiri dan menerima bahawa skizofrenia adalah sesuatu yang perlu diurus sepanjang hidup.
Fitri mengambil ubat mengikut nasihat doktor, sambil menjaga tidur, dan mengubah beberapa aspek kehidupan bagi mengawal perkara yang boleh mencetuskan gejala skizofrenia, selain mendalami agama.
Apabila diminta menggambarkan kestabilan kehidupannya sekarang berbanding dahulu, berpandukan skala satu hingga sepuluh, Fitri menjawab: "Daripada 10, saya di tahap ke sembilan".

Salah satu rutinnya ialah berkongsi secebis kehidupannya di TikTok sejak 2023, menceritakan serba-serbi cabaran yang pernah dan sedang beliau hadapi, sekaligus mendekatkan penonton dengan pengamalan sebenar seorang pesakit skizofrenia.
Dalam satu video pada Ogos, Fitri menceritakan bahawa beliau kurang mengikuti kandungan di media sosial lain kerana tidak mahu emosi terganggu, sebaliknya lebih menggemari senaskah buku.
"Dulu saya fikir orang lain kena faham saya. Tapi lama-lama saya sedar, saya pun kena faham diri saya sendiri," kata pemuda dari Tapah, Perak ini.
Fitri tidak mahu pesakit skizofrenia hanya dilihat sebagai golongan yang perlu dikasihani, menegaskan bahawa mereka perlu diberi ruang untuk berdikari.

"Ironinya tempat kerja adalah ruang selamat saya. Jadi rakan sekerja hampir tidak perasan pun saya sedang bergelut dengan penyakit mental. Sekarang mereka sudah tahu, dan sedang belajar menerimanya," katanya.

Pakar psikiatri, Dr Fakrul Azren Azhar, yang mengenali Fitri menerusi beberapa sesi audio siar berkaitan skizofrenia, berkata beliau kagum dengan usaha Fitri dan keberanian beliau berkongsi pengalamannya secara terbuka.

"Pulih itu subjektif sebenarnya. Kita bukan nak simptom dia hilang semata-mata, tetapi keupayaan dia untuk menjalani kehidupan seperti orang normal. Kualiti hidup itu yang kita nak capai sebenarnya," katanya.
Pada 2024, Malaysia merekodkan 8,303 kes skizofrenia, manakala hospital awam mencatatkan peningkatan kes sebanyak 14.6% berbanding 2021, menurut Menteri Kesihatan Dzulkefly Ahmad.
33c35dfafca606c0: ISTANBUL: Indonesia has recorded 333,470 cases of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) linked to forest and land fires in several regions, the Health Ministry said on Thursday.
The ministry's director of environmental health, Then Suyanti, said daily cases remained high, with 4,522 new cases reported, Anadolu Ajansi reported, citing state-run news agency Antara.

She said the latest Air Pollutant Index showed that air quality in several areas had reached hazardous levels, particularly in six provinces prioritised for fire management: Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, South Kalimantan and Central Kalimantan.

Suyanti said exposure to wildfire smoke, which contains fine particulate matter such as PM2.5, carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide and other organic compounds, can cause health problems, including ARIs, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, eye and skin irritation, and other systemic health effects.

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said on Thursday that if foreign-backed companies were responsible for recurring forest and land fires, they could lose their operating permits, and revoked concessions could be reassigned to younger Indonesians.

"Regarding forest fires, there are indications that many foreign companies bear responsibility. They have held concessions for over a decade, yet some have committed violations three, four, or even a dozen times — some as many as 19 times," Prabowo said, adding that their permits should be revoked if they committed two violations.

Separately, thousands of students and others demonstrated in Samarinda, the capital of East Kalimantan, demanding that the government declare forest and land fires a national disaster, according to iNews.
Indonesia is experiencing an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Niño contributing to conditions favourable for wildfires.
36af9f8fc23ea6f1: BELGRADE: Around 150,000 supporters of Serbia's opposition student movement rallied in central Belgrade on Thursday, seeking to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in crunch parliamentary elections this weekend.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, wants to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in Sunday's vote.

It is the biggest threat Vucic has faced and civil society groups have warned the poll campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests, attacks, misuse of public resources and a distorted media environment.

"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told AFP as she arrived for the students' rally.
"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible," she said.
Around 150,000 people gathered at the Student List rally on Thursday evening in Belgrade, the independent crowd size monitoring group the Archive of Public Gatherings said in a post on X.
The vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.

Waving "Students are winning" flags, chanting, and blowing whistles, students and their supporters marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
They filled the square and the surrounding streets, according to AFP reporters.

"We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours," university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd, who chanted "Victory, victory!"
"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!," he said.
The rally ended with the candidates stepping down from the stage into the crowd while holding the Serbian constitution in their hands before dancing a traditional folk dance with supporters.
Vucic defiant
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, Vucic announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
"Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!" he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.

Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic from Belgrade University told AFP it was difficult to predict an outcome but expected students to win more than 40% of the vote, a result significantly larger than any opposition list since SNS came to power.
Threats, intimidation
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for "free and fair elections" were lacking.
"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said.
"It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organisations working in different fields."
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting "violence, riots and attacks" on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
"I've been following this fight since the very beginning," 35-year-old student rally attendee Igor said.
"Today is the last rally, and it's important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations," Igor added.
52aab20f61d0332e: KUALA LUMPUR: S. Sivasangari will face giant-killer Anahat Singh of India after brushing aside compatriot Rachel Arnold to reach the Silicon Valley Open semi-finals in the United States on Thursday.
