32da3eb9d3a9ff61: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 23 — Budget 2027 is officially out, bringing a much-needed financial lifeline to Malaysians feeling the pinch of rising living costs.

Whether you are a gig worker looking to buy your first home, a parent managing back-to-school expenses, or a B40 household needing a monthly cash boost, the latest national budget packs targeted relief for almost everyone.
Here is your complete guide to the assistance schemes you can tap into next year.
Direct cash transfers: STR and SARA payouts
The Rahmah initiatives remain the foundation of the government’s welfare strategy, channelling direct support to lower-income households.
Under Budget 2027, Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) provides up to RM150 a month, capping at RM1,800 annually for Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) recipients.
Adult Malaysians missing out on STR will also not walk away empty-handed. They will receive a total of RM200 through two RM100 SARA Madani payouts.
STR recipients (Monthly SARA)
Who qualifies: Approved STR recipients.
Amount: Up to RM150 a month, totalling RM1,800 a year.
How to use: The government credits the funds directly to your MyKad. You can spend this at participating shops, supermarkets, and FAMA farmers’ markets to buy approved daily necessities.
How to apply: Verify your status or update your details via the official MySTR portal.
Non-STR recipients (SARA Madani)
Who qualifies: Malaysian citizens aged 18 and above who do not receive STR.
Amount: RM200 total for the year.
Payout schedule: Expect RM100 just before Hari Raya Aidilfitri and another RM100 ahead of Merdeka.
Education aid: Bigger Bantuan Awal Persekolahan payouts

To ease the perennial headache of back-to-school expenses, the government is increasing the Bantuan Awal Persekolahan (BAP) cash aid. Parents will now receive a one-off payment of RM200 per student, a welcome increase from the previous RM150.

Schools will distribute these funds directly at the start of the academic year. Crucially, this aid ignores income brackets and household size. It covers 5.3 million Malaysian students from Year 1 through Form 5 across government, religious, and registered private schools.
Housing perks: Stamp duty waivers and gig worker loans
Budget 2027 slashes the hefty upfront costs of buying a house and opens doors for Malaysians lacking traditional payslips.

Stamp duty exemptions: First-time homebuyers unlock massive savings. The government offers a full stamp duty waiver for properties priced up to RM500,000, and a partial waiver for homes up to RM750,000. Buying a RM500,000 house instantly saves you between RM10,000 and RM15,000.

SJKP financing guarantees: Gig workers, petty traders, and freelancers often struggle to secure mortgages. To fix this, the government is injecting RM20 billion into the Syarikat Jaminan Kredit Perumahan (SJKP) scheme. By acting as the ultimate guarantor, the government helps self-employed Malaysians secure bank loans that would normally face rejection.
Small business support: Cheaper rent for KL hawkers
To keep operational costs manageable for micro-entrepreneurs, the budget extends a crucial lifeline to grassroots traders in the capital.
Vendors operating in licensed Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) hawker stalls, markets, and food courts will continue enjoying a 50 per cent discount on their monthly rent.
This relief extends the existing programme, benefiting 10,000 small business premises through to December 2027.
How to check your eligibility
While Budget 2027 casts a wide safety net, your exact eligibility depends heavily on your household status and updated income data.
You can verify your specific entitlements and check your status by logging into the official portal at using your MyKad number.
3592bd3a894982eb: BANGKOK, Oct 23 — After months of fires in Indonesia that have caused thick regional haze, attention is turning to whether companies can be held accountable for the blazes and resulting air pollution.

Indonesia experiences fires regularly during its dry season, and experts say years of deforestation and the draining of peatland for cultivation have rendered previously fire-resistant landscapes vulnerable.

Driven by a strong El Nino cycle and resulting drought, this year’s blazes have been particularly severe, burning through nearly two million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.
The fires have raged across forests and peatland but also palm oil and timber plantations supplying multinational firms.
Civil society groups have regularly accused companies of responsibility for the blazes, pointing to so-called “hotspots” in supplier plantations, sometimes called concessions.
Environmental group WALHI says it mapped “high confidence” hotspots across Indonesia using NASA fire data and found around 50 per cent were inside concessions.
In a report this month the group listed 40 timber and palm oil concessions by the number of hotspots detected.
“This is a structural issue... (that) happens because of the practices, the activities, of these companies,” WALHI forests and plantations campaigner Umi Ma’rufah told AFP.
Pressure is also coming from governments, including Singapore, which has issued 10 companies with “preventative measure notices” under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
The notices urge them to fight fires on their land, prevent burning and submit action plans. Firms can face legal action including fines if they do not comply.
“We must also be clear about where the responsibility for this lies,” Singapore Senior Minister K. Shanmugam told reporters.
“This was not simply an act of nature, but a problem driven by companies pursuing profits.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Firefighters and residents use hoses to extinguish spreading wildfires amid dense smoke and a hazy sunset in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan province on October 21, 2026. — AFP pic
Legal liability
Several companies implicated have insisted they are not behind the fires.

“Fires originating outside our boundaries subsequently spread into areas under the Group’s management,” Singapore Exchange-listed palm oil company First Resources said after one of its concessions was listed in WALHI’s report.

Asia Pulp and Paper, a Singapore-registered firm, also insisted that fires in supplier concessions do not “necessarily mean that land was deliberately burned or that the concession holder was responsible for starting the fire.”
Satellite monitoring can sometimes show where fires started, said Nusantara Atlas founder David Gaveau.
“In some cases, the satellite photos clearly show that fire starts inside, but we cannot say whether it’s by design or whether it’s accidental,” he told AFP.
“In other cases it’s also clear that fire started outside and spread inside the concession.”
Experts say fire has been used in the past to illegally open up land for cultivation, including in large concessions, but also by smaller-scale local investors.
Parts of Indonesia also previously allowed smallholders to use fire to clear plots of land, though this year the government has cracked down on that practice too.
Even if fires begin accidentally or outside concessions, firms may have legal responsibilities, explained Azam Hawari, a lawyer with environmental law NGO ClientEarth.
“An external source of ignition or extreme weather does not necessarily absolve a company of civil liability,” said Hawari.

Companies are required to have sufficient fire measures, including personnel and equipment, and could also be liable “where activities pose a serious threat to the environment,” like peatland drainage, he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Motorcyclists navigate a road heavily obscured by thick haze from nearby forest and land fires in Tegal Arum, Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan on October 20, 2026. — AFP pic
International links
Indonesia has announced “administrative sanctions” against dozens of firms and criminal proceedings against 125 individuals and corporations.
But campaigner Umi pointed out that some previously prosecuted firms have failed to pay fines or carry out forest restoration.
“It’s about the will from the government to really do their (enforcement) task,” she said.
Some implicated concessions have ties well behind Indonesia’s borders, said Holly Yang, an accounting professor at Singapore Management University who teaches sustainability reporting.
After WALHI’s report, she and her student Ashmit Bansal mapped concession holders, owners, creditors, investors and supply-chain partners.
“The fires occur in Indonesia, but the ownership, financing and commercial relationships extend across borders,” Yang told AFP.
Yang noted that a connection “does not, by itself, establish responsibility for a fire”.
But mapping relationships “allows the public to ask informed questions and assess how those parties respond”. — AFP
eae3e36085783365: TAIPEI, Oct 23 — Taiwan has been waiting months for US President Donald Trump to approve a US$14 billion (RM57 billion) sale of weapons and equipment, which the island democracy would use to fend off a potential Chinese attack.
Washington – Taipei’s most important security backer – has sold many billions of dollars’ worth of arms to Taiwan, most recently in December when it approved a record US$11.1 billion package.
China opposes American military support for Taiwan, which Beijing claims is part of its territory and has threatened to seize with force.

Trump, who last month hailed his “great friendship” with Chinese President Xi Jinping, has resisted US political pressure, including from Republican lawmakers, to give the green light for the current arms package.
AFP takes a look at what’s in it and why it’s being held up:
Why is Taiwan buying US arms?
Taiwan is spending huge sums upgrading its defence capabilities and expanding its domestic weapons production capacity, but it still needs US arms to deter China.

Since Washington switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1979, the United States has stuck to its commitments under the Taiwan Relations Act to provide weapons to Taiwan for its defence.
But Trump said in May that US arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, setting off alarm bells across the world.
Taipei has reminded Trump of US commitments, and US officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio have insisted American policy on Taiwan has not changed.

The sale would signal US support for Taiwan and send a message to Beijing that if it launched an attack, it would not face “Taiwan alone”, said Wang Ting-yu, a senior lawmaker in President Lai Ching-te’s Democratic Progressive Party.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A Taiwanese military Patriot missile system is deployed at a local park during the annual Han Kuang military exercise in New Taipei City on August 6, 2026. — AFP pic
What’s in the package?
Taiwan is developing a multi-layered air defence system, known as the T-Dome, that it hopes could counter a potential Chinese attack.

Patriot missiles, an automated command and control system and a 360-degree air defence radar system are seen as critical components of this system and are among the items in the US$14 billion package.
“Together these systems can strengthen the resilience of Taiwan’s strategic air defences,” said Su Tzu-yun, a military expert at the Taipei-based Institute for National Defense and Security Research.
Money for the weapons system is expected to come from a US$25 billion defence spending bill passed by Taiwan’s parliament in May after months of political wrangling.
Why has it been delayed?
Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May – the first of four expected meetings for 2026 – as the rival leaders sought to ease trade tensions between their countries.
Xi issued a blunt warning to Trump that missteps on Taiwan could push the US and China into “conflict”.
A record US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan could threaten the US-China trade truce.
“I’m going to make a determination. I’m going to see,” Trump said after the summit in response to a question about whether he would go ahead with arms sales to Taiwan.
Rubio said in June that the proposed package was “under review”, while officials said in May they were assessing whether American weapons stockpiles were sufficient for its Iran operations.
A US official said recently that the chances of the package being split into smaller chunks “have gone way up”.
Some Taiwanese officials have said they do not care if the US bundles the arms into a single package or multiple – they just want the weapons.
“Militarily... Taiwan is racing against time,” said the analyst Su.
“Acquiring weapons is not like ordering at a drive-through. Production, delivery and training all take time before the systems can enter service and become effective.” — AFP
f578f46c50e9f804: BRUSSELS, Oct 23 — Thick or thin, greasy or crispy, with samurai sauce or a more traditional mayo dip? A TV show has been on a quest to find the best fries in potato-mad Belgium.

For four years running “La meilleure friterie” (the best chip shop), a lighthearted culinary competition aired by broadcaster RTL-TVI, has been seeking out perfection among fry peddlers in the country’s French-speaking region.
Watching it is a “sacred Thursday night ritual”, said David Antoine, the host.
Crowning a winner among a dozen contestants is no picnic.

“There’s sometimes friction among the judges, but we always find that famous Belgian compromise” over a portion of fries, Antoine told AFP in a joking reference to the country’s penchant for lengthy political negotiations.
Fried potatoes are a national dish and symbol of pride in Belgium, home to about 4,600 diners specialising in the dish known as “friteries” in French or “frituren” in Flemish.
That number “has remained stable for many years,” said Bernard Lefevre of the National Chip Shop Union, an industry group, noting the “market is doing well”.
Each has its own flair.
To Lefevre, a good chip is preferably cut from a Belgian potato of the Bintje variety and double fried in beef fat. And size is paramount.
“Anything under nine millimetres is too thin and anything over fourteen is too thick,” he explained.
Hand-peeled ‘gold’
At Hill’s Burger, a diner in Brussels, chef Massimo Sefa has gone for a “size twelve”—that is “a two-millimetre crust and ten millimetres of creamy flesh”, he said.
The 23-year-old smiled nervously when the TV show’s judges entered his joint and the cameras started rolling.
But the stress is worth it, he explained. The broadcast will shine a spotlight on his friterie and a win would likely send sales skyrocketing.
Sefa opened up shop with his two younger brothers, Lorenzo and Marco. For them chips are a family matter: their grandfather ran about 10 chip shops in Brussels.
“Wow, delicious, crispy, and peeled by hand,” Fabienne De Corte, one of the judges, raved upon tasting the goods.
“Fries in Belgium are our gold,” added her husband Patrick De Corte, who is also on the judging panel.
“Every little detail makes a difference.”
The show has a devout following, including some who tag along for filming sometimes dressed as fry cones and chanting “We’ve got the fries, we’ve got the potatoes!”.
It has also had its share of controversies, particularly on the hot topic of sauces.
A technical glitch caused trouble during public voting in the first season and some grumbled the winner had bamboozled jurors with dazzling sauces, while the fries were not to everyone’s taste.
Still the show has established itself in the French-speaking Belgian media landscape at a time where fries are sometimes changing along with Belgian society.
“There are halal, vegetarian, and vegan fry shops—that’s perfectly normal; society is evolving. We’re not a museum of bygone folklore,” Lefevre insists. — AFP
dc93cff7fe8da5f5: TOKYO, Oct 23 — Artificial intelligence has found critical security flaws in a major programming language called PHP, with many websites taken offline Thursday as organisations worldwide scramble to fend off would-be hackers.
As AI’s fast-advancing capabilities fuel concern over the increased risk of cyberattacks, here are some questions and answers about the situation:
What is PHP and how widely used is it?
Created in the early 1990s, PHP is a computer programming language that helps run an estimated 70 per cent of the world’s websites.
It is “a backbone of the web”, according to security firm Wiz Research, which says it used AI to find vulnerabilities hidden in PHP for more than a decade.

PHP – a name that originally stood for Personal Home Page – underpins popular web design platforms, meaning the flaws could allow hackers to break into various sites, from online stores to government services.
A fix was released Wednesday, with the PHP Foundation telling the tech departments of companies and organisations around the world: “If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now.”
That has resulted in a slew of apps and websites – from the Paris police website to a Pokemon sleep tracker – going dark as developers work to protect their underlying code from hacks.
How did AI find the flaws?
Cutting-edge AI models, such as those from US giants OpenAI and Google, were used by Wiz and other groups to uncover PHP’s weak spots in August.
This was kept under wraps while a fix was developed.
OpenAI called the flaws “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory”, adding that it “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact”.
Separately to Wiz, security firm Calif found the flaws as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.

“The trouble with tools like AI is that the moment all the information’s out there, people can weaponise it very, very quickly,” Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, told AFP.
“That’s why everybody’s acting with such urgency to respond to this issue.”
Have sites already been hacked?

“Taking websites offline does not necessarily mean they have been hacked. It can be a responsible measure to protect systems while security updates are applied,” said Dimitrios Salampasis from Australia’s Swinburne University of Technology.
So far “the evidence that security researchers are seeing is that nobody was actively performing attacks using the techniques available”, Kerrison said.
Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to fix their websites relatively quickly – but others may be left vulnerable.
“There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won’t for days, weeks and months,” Kerrison warned.
That may include user-run blogs that could be used to spread computer viruses, spam people or distribute malicious content.
Could there be other consequences?
A data breach could affect customers in the future if their personal information is used in so-called “phishing” attacks, where someone is tricked into revealing their password to an online service.
The complex and interlinked nature of online systems, which often use third-party interfaces, means some vulnerabilities could remain even after the problem is fixed.
If the third parties use PHP, “then even though you patched yourself... you’re still unsecure”, said Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cyber security at the University of New South Wales, Sydney.
PHP isn’t everything, however – strong cybersecurity measures should include several layers of defences, Kerrison said. — AFP
9a4e40fe29b83e22: PETALING JAYA: Gengsterisme dalam kalangan masyarakat India lazim berakar umbi di sekolah menengah, dengan pelajar yang lemah akademik serta terpinggir paling terdedah direkrut, menurut sebuah buku baharu.
Penulisnya yang juga aktivis sosial, Janakey Raman Manickam, berkata pelajar India yang kurang keyakinan dan arah tuju lazim menyertai geng untuk merasakan diri diterima dan diiktiraf.
Katanya, sebaik direkrut, remaja berkenaan dibayar untuk melakukan jenayah.

Janakey yang banyak menulis mengenai isu melibatkan masyarakat India di Malaysia berkata, ramai remaja seperti itu terjebak jenayah kecil untuk menampakkan imej ‘macho’, menarik perhatian rakan sebaya, atau mendapat duit poket.
“Lebih banyak jenayah dilakukan, lebih hebat kedudukan mereka dalam geng,” katanya dalam buku bertajuk ‘Malaysian Indians: Impact and Pain: Narration of an Unending Saga of a Marginalised Community’.
Janakey berkata, pelajar seperti ini lazimnya semakin terjerumus dalam jenayah berat termasuk merompak dan mengedar dadah.
Beliau turut mempertikai sistem pendidikan yang dianggapnya terlampau memberi tekanan terhadap pelajar cemerlang tetapi membiarkan pelajar lemah tanpa sokongan diperlukan.

“Secara tidak langsung, pelajar lemah daripada masyarakat India ketinggalan. Selalunya mereka tersisih di sekolah kerana tidak ramai guru mempedulikan mereka,” katanya, menambah pelajar seperti itu lazim dilabel pencetus masalah.
Janakey berkata, walaupun wujud latihan vokasional dan kemahiran, ramai pelajar meninggalkan sekolah menengah tanpa menyedari peluang yang terbuka untuk mereka.
Beliau mendesak mereka diberi lebih perhatian dan dipimpin ke arah kerjaya lebih baik, seiring langkah-langkah bagi meningkatkan kestabilan kewangan untuk keluarga berpendapatan rendah.
Katanya, gengsterisme dalam kalangan masyarakat India kini mencapai tahap kritikal, dan sudah tiba masa untuk ancaman ini ditangani menerusi perancangan serius serta tindakan tegas.
Menurut laporan pada 2013, 38 daripada 29 pertubuhan rahsia dan sindiket jenayah yang disenaraihitamkan kerajaan banyak dioperasikan pemuda India.
Pada 2021, naib presiden MIC ketika itu C Sivarraajh berkata orang India merangkumi 28,926 atau hampir 72% daripada ahli geng yang dikenal pasti di seluruh negara.
d1f540bef4b10c9e: PETALING JAYA: For nearly four decades, Rumah Ozanam has offered vulnerable children more than just a roof over their heads - it has given them stability, care and the chance to build a better future.
Located on Jalan Padang here, the home has supported hundreds of children over the years, many from impoverished or troubled family backgrounds.

Today, its own future has become uncertain. Donations have dwindled while operating costs continue to mount, leaving the charitable organisation struggling to care for the young people who depend on it.

“We are in dire straits; our current bank balance is only around RM2,000," Rumah Ozanam board president Gabriel Bala Murali told FMT Lifestyle. "As our funds are nearly exhausted, our need is extremely urgent."
Established on March 22, 1987, Rumah Ozanam actually runs two homes - one for boys and another for girls - providing shelter to children who have experienced poverty, abandonment, neglect or abuse.
At present, it has 15 residents - 11 girls and four boys aged between eight and 17.

Many of the children come from struggling families, including single-parent households and homes where parents are unable to work because of health problems. Others are referred there by the social welfare department through the courts.
Beyond accommodation, Rumah Ozanam tries to give its residents the routines and stability of an ordinary childhood.

Their days begin early, with breakfast at 6am before they leave for school at around 6.45am. After returning in the afternoon, they have lunch, rest and complete household chores, while evenings are set aside for games, tuition and study.
The home also arranges extracurricular activities, including football and tennis lessons conducted by volunteers, while counselling is available when needed.
Education remains one of Rumah Ozanam’s biggest priorities. Besides covering school supplies, transportation and tuition, it also supports deserving residents who wish to pursue higher education.

For Gabriel, seeing former residents graduate and move forward with their lives is among the most rewarding parts of the work. "It shows that our efforts to better a child’s life have paid off,” he said.

Keeping that lifeline going, however, has become increasingly difficult. Gabriel said Rumah Ozanam once received steady contributions from corporate sponsors, individual donors and other well-wishers, but much of that support fell away following the pandemic.
Rumah Ozanam needs about RM25,000 a month to cover food, school supplies, staff salaries, utilities, maintenance and other daily expenses.
A fundraising dinner is planned for April 2027, but the more immediate concern is securing enough money to get through the coming months.
Gabriel said an emergency contribution of RM60,000 would provide much-needed breathing room while the home works towards greater financial stability.
He hopes individuals, companies and other well-wishers will step forward, whether through one-off donations or regular monthly contributions.
“We want nothing more than to ensure our children continue to have a safe, secure and loving home where they can heal and grow,” he concluded.
If you wish to help, donations can be made to CIMB bank account 800 230 4523 (Yayasan Ozanam - SVP Rumah Ozanam). Tax-exemption receipts will be provided for donations of RM50 and above.
Learn more about Rumah Ozanam on Facebook. For further information, contact Gabriel at 03-7781 9013 or 012-607 0837.
783063192087e7f7: PETALING JAYA: Gangsterism among Malaysian Indians often takes root in secondary school, with academically weaker and marginalised students particularly vulnerable to gang recruitment, a new book reveals.
Its author and prominent social activist Janakey Raman Manickam said Indian students who lack confidence and direction often join gangs in search of acceptance and recognition.
Once recruited, these teenagers are paid to commit crimes, he said.
Janakey, who has written extensively on issues affecting Malaysian Indians, said many of these teenagers turn to petty crime to project a macho image, impress their peers or earn pocket money.
"The more crimes they commit, the better their position in the gang," he wrote in a book, titled “Malaysian Indians: Impact and Pain: Narration of an Unending Saga of a Marginalised Community”.
Janakey said these students often progress to more serious crimes, including robbery and drug trafficking.
He also questioned the education system, saying it places too much emphasis on high achievers while leaving weaker students without adequate support.
“Indirectly, low achievers from the Indian community are ‘swept out’,” he said.
“They are usually marginalised at school because not many teachers are concerned about them,” he added, noting that these students are often labelled “problem makers”.
Janakey said despite the availability of vocational and skills training, many students leave secondary school unaware of the opportunities available to them.
“These students are clueless,” he said, urging that they be given greater attention and better career guidance alongside measures to enhance the financial stability of low-income families.
Janakey said gangsterism among the Indian community has reached a critical stage.
The time has come for the menace to be addressed with serious planning and decisive action, he said.
In 2013, it was reported that 38 of the 49 active secret societies and criminal syndicates blacklisted by the government were predominantly operated by Indian youths.
In 2021, then MIC vice-president C Sivarraajh, said Indians accounted for 28,926, or nearly 72%, of identified gang members nationwide.

a1d2ae5272788d7b: WASHINGTON: Elon Musk said this week that SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to study a merger of his two biggest companies.
The combination would be worth about US$3.5 trillion and would be the largest corporate deal in history.
What is SpaceX?
Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 to cut the cost of reaching space and one day bring humans to Mars.

Its reusable Falcon 9 rockets dominate the global launch market, its Dragon capsule carries Nasa astronauts to the International Space Station, and its Starlink satellite network provides internet service worldwide.

The company is no longer just a rocket maker. In February, it absorbed xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence (AI) startup - known for its Grok chatbot - which had taken over the social network X in 2025.
SpaceX went public this year in a record listing and is now valued at about US$2 trillion.
Much of its recent growth comes from renting data centre computing power to other AI companies.
What is Tesla?
Tesla was founded in 2003 and became the world’s best-known electric carmaker after Musk became chief executive in 2008. It is valued at about US$1.5 trillion.
Its core car business has come under pressure and Musk increasingly presents Tesla as a company built around self-driving robotaxis and its Optimus humanoid robot.
Why merge?
Musk told analysts Tuesday that a merger would be "a good idea".
Florian Frischmuth of engineering consultancy Envorso said a combined group could centrally control the key ingredients of AI - chips, energy and connectivity.
Garrett Nelson of CFRA Research wrote in a note that synergies would likely be small relative to the size of the deal, which in his view would mostly be about control.
Musk holds about 82 percent of SpaceX’s voting power but only about 20% at Tesla, where his moves have drawn scrutiny and lawsuits from investors.
How easy will it be?
Most analysts expect a deal.
"In our view once Musk discussed the deal it’s a matter of when and not if this happens," Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives told AFP.
He put the odds at 90% by early 2027 and said Tesla would likely need to be valued at more than US$500 per share to win approval.
Musk cautioned that a merger is not certain. It needs the support of a majority of all Tesla shares, which he called "quite a high hurdle".
However, Nelson noted that loyal retail investors hold an estimated 25% to 27% of Tesla shares. With Musk’s stake added, only a small portion of institutional investors would need to back the deal.
The legal obstacles appear slight because both companies moved their incorporation from Delaware to Texas, according to Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado.
In Texas, shareholders challenging a deal must first show fraud or intentional misconduct, and companies can require that certain suits be brought only by holders of 3% of the stock.
At SpaceX, that means about US$60 billion of stock.
"I think Musk will have no trouble getting a deal through from a corporate perspective," Lipton said. "He should be able to muscle something through," Lipton added.
What are the obstacles?
Lipton said the bigger risks lie in SpaceX’s importance to the US government and Tesla’s operations in China.
SpaceX depends heavily on contracts with Nasa and the Pentagon, and Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican campaigns.
Analysts say that if Democrats regain power in Washington, investigations into Musk’s companies could resume, and SpaceX could eventually find government contracts harder to win.
Musk has warned Democrats against targeting him if they return to power.
"Live by the sword, die by the sword," he wrote on X, responding to a report on Democrats’ plans to investigate his activities if they win the midterms.
Tesla's large China manufacturing base could also draw national security scrutiny.
One option, JPMorgan analysts said, would be to wall off Tesla’s China business or hand control of it to a China-based consortium, similar to the arrangement for TikTok in the US.

4a7fb2460297143f: A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."

The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.

Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.

712bc0d815dcfe0f: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.

That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”

Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.
Start with the workload, not the model
There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.

A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.
The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.

That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.

A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t.

The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost.
Engineer the system, not the model

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements.

For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.
Build for change, not today’s benchmark

Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.
The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

88e73b340e5cf3c4: As a child, you likely saw a few Disney movies depicting inanimate objects, such as clocks, cups, and toys, as interactive companions to humans — an act of pure magic, seemingly. But scientists at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) are now doing something similar: transforming stationary items into self-aware tools that perceive and respond to human motion to complete a task. Engineers have 3D-printed these dynamic items with built-in sensing, using conductive materials for sensors and traces (sort of like wires) inside. The issue: both components were typically fabricated using the same material, so they’d emit similar signals. It’s sort of like hearing two radio stations at the same time, a mixup that’s hard to interpret. This confuses, say, a glove that relays instructions to a robotic hand about how to handle a specific object. The device couldn’t filter out the noise or verify the angle of a user’s motions, leading a humanoid student to make errors. Researchers at CSAIL and Tianjin University (TJU) in China may have found a way to 3D print more precise interactive items. With their “X-Hinges” software, users can customize a design, and the tool will automatically embed two different materials: a filament for the sensors designed to send the strongest signal possible, and another for the wire-like elements that don’t interfere. Interactions won’t get lost in translation, meaning users can fabricate objects that respond in real-time, such as small robots, household decor, object-detection systems, and toys. With X-Hinges, users can put together an item by selecting and connecting different shapes, then choosing how certain parts move. The item won’t be limited to moving in just one way like previous approaches; instead, users can select up to three “axes:” compressing, up and down, or to the sides. Building a robotic hand, for example, you’d likely want its fingertips to move vertically and laterally. The new tool would then embed sensors where the object bends (in this case, its joints) to capture motion data from both angles. That way, the device can understand and respond to your interactions more dynamically once it’s 3D-printed. “It’s kind of like adding a conscious element to everyday objects,” says Jiaji Li, MIT electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) postdoc and CSAIL researcher, who is a senior author on a paper introducing the work. “What you get is objects that better understand how they’re being used and have more ways to respond. In the same way an AI agent is programmed to make certain decisions based on our instructions, these creations have built-in sensing to adaptively react to human touch.” Jiaji Li and lead author Xiang Chang, a TJU PhD student and visiting researcher at CSAIL, used X-Hinges to create many clever devices. For example, they made a glove that can teach a robot how to grasp blocks. It adjusts to the size of a user’s hands, then records how the joints in their fingers bend via sensors before rapidly relaying that information to a humanoid hand to mimic it. The glove could be useful in factories or homes, where a robot often needs to learn new interactions quickly. The researchers also produced a small, origami-style lamp using X-Hinges. It senses when a human pinches it closed and adjusts its brightness accordingly. When you turn on this adaptive, portable light source (sort of like a reading light), it looks like a piece of folded-up paper that sprouts into a lamp. X-Hinges can even assemble devices that identify which objects have been placed on it. You could put a banana on top, for instance, and it’ll recognize the fruit almost immediately based on the tactile data it’s recorded using its sensors. This advanced physical awareness could be integrated into detection systems in places such as airports and grocery stores.  Behind each of the scientists’ creations is an easy-to-use interface that helps you design interactive objects from scratch. Users can choose how each part of their design looks and moves, just as the researchers did when making a video game controller that resembles a cartoon shark. X-Hinges gives you four shapes to choose from: a custom option, cylinder, rectangle, and thin outline. To recreate the unique look of a shark’s tail, the researchers designed their own shape. They then chose how the toy bent, opting for its tail to move up and down, sort of like a joystick. Finally, the program embedded the sensors, and the scientists 3D-printed their device. The researchers say that X-Hinges’ diverse motions are a novel feature compared to past attempts to 3D-print responsive everyday objects. “Most methods only allow for one axis of motion, often due to signal interference. X-Hinges enables your 3D-printed item to move from three angles,” says Chang. “Ultimately, you get a design with the intended movement you want. It also records motion data in each of those areas at the same time, making the device responsive to different kinds of interactions.” The tool could help realize the untapped potential of the seemingly mundane. Objects we use every day for a specific purpose, like a water bottle for drinking or a lamp for lighting, could become interactive gadgets. Much like how a chatbot uses a sort of digital intelligence to answer your prompts, an object could leverage a kind of physical intelligence to execute a physical task when users interact with it. For now, though, X-Hinges faces a calibration bottleneck. Each time an item is 3D-printed, its layout of electrical elements varies slightly, so two devices that appear identical from the outside may not make the same sensor readings. This is crucial if you’re building a deformable fitness glove, for instance, for two separate users. To fix this, Chang and Li built a computer vision system that can recalibrate outputs to align, ensuring data is accurate across two of the same items, although they hope to develop a built-in signal recalibration mechanism in the future. That ambition traces back to the throughline in Jiaji Li’s own research: letting actuation and sensing “grow” directly inside a 3D-printed object, instead of adding them on afterward. He previously built printed tendon-driven mechanisms that gave objects the ability to move; X-Hinges is how he’s now building on the ability to sense. The next step, he says, is combining the two in a single print — it’s actuation and sensing born together in the same fabrication process, opening the door to new physical platforms for embodied intelligence and AI agents. Chang and Li wrote the paper with MIT associate professor of EECS and CSAIL principal investigator Stefanie Mueller and recent TJU graduate Haiyang Yan. Their work was supported, in part, by a postdoctoral research fellowship from Zhejiang University and the MIT-GIST Program. The researchers will present their work at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in early November.
7792da17809db852: Researchers have developed a new exploit that shows how even Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on an x86-64 server cannot stop the PHP2Shell vulnerability. VulnCheck, which made it available to only the company’s Initial Access Intelligence customers, also warned that threat actors are using AI to find even more ways to attack.

The team told us that it’s a “significant advance” because up until now, ASLR has been a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on real-world servers. They don't expect that to hold, though. “Adversaries are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug,” Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register.
The PHP2Shell mess grew even bigger on Thursday amid reports of attackers abusing the security flaws days before they were disclosed and UK government websites proactively going dark.

Vulncheck's exploit targets CVE-2026-109618, a critical, out-of-memory corruption bug that leads to remote code execution (RCE) in PHP, and part of the PHP2Shell pair alongside CVE-2026-109619. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and issued patches for both on Wednesday.

Overnight, VulnCheck researchers developed what they believe is the first known exploit to achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration.

ASLR is a built-in defense against memory-corruption bugs – like PHP2Shell – that randomly arranges memory locations of a program's key data areas. By scrambling these components live, in memory every time a program runs, ASLR prevents an attacker trying to achieve RCE from correctly guessing the target memory address – and thus prevents them from executing malicious code.
While VulnCheck has seen “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, “very few contain legitimate, working exploits,” McIntyre told us, adding that this is largely due to ASLR.

“There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” McIntyre said. “One of the biggest obstacles has been ASLR, a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.”

The threat hunters’ new technique, we’re told, bypasses ASLR. It uses a confirmed memory leak chained into RCE on PHP 8.4.26, and they claim it works on x86-64 platforms even with ASLR enabled and PHP’s recommended display_errors=off production configuration.

“We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions,” McIntyre said. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome.”
VulnCheck says it also works on ARM64, but the RCE is not currently functional on ARM-based systems.

This should be a wake-up call to all organizations that, especially now in the era of AI bug hunting and exploit development, “the technical difficulty of exploiting a vulnerability shouldn't be confused with protection against it,” McIntyre said.
“Organizations running vulnerable versions of PHP should prioritize patching rather than assume existing memory protections or configuration changes will stop an attack.” ®

f80ad67e809508ad: Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet.

Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement.

These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria.

Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective.

Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests.

Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from.

“The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.”

Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything.

It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. The AI model “performed competitively” against a specialized model at predicting phage-host interactions, the research write-up notes.
There’s nothing in the paper to suggest the patient was suffering from a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.

“This marks an important milestone in translating AI-designed biology from computational predictions and laboratory validation to clinical administration,” Radical Numerics said of its work. The treatment takes the technology beyond laboratory testing, even if it turns out not to fully eliminate the infection. Radical Numerics hopes its work will lead to a process for designing and building phages targeted to individual bacterial infections, and the need for alternatives is already pressing – antibiotic resistance is a growing global health threat, with drug-resistant infections already causing substantial mortality worldwide.
Radical Numerics didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

edf0f2f0c25d5525: Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense.

A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning.
The technique, dubbed MuTRAP, is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.

MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills.
The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006.

"Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service.
"It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources."

The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word.

The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B.

Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper.

No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine.

But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's proposed defense known as PROTEA, which employs an LLM to judge and evaluate the security of task plans (and should not be confused with several other research projects named PROTEA).

There are already ample real-world examples of robots that have violated the first of science fiction writer Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics – "A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm." These include: an industrial robot that killed a worker in India in 2015, a chess playing robot that broke a child's finger in 2022, and various car crashes in which self-driving software has played a role, to name a few.
Of course, Asimov's "laws" are not actually laws. They're just fictional rules. ®

55fbeed2b08e6c9f: A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.

Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.

c3c91acfa9688b51: GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now.

The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264, affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014.

The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes.

GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.”

GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections (here and here) for customers with self-managed instances.
Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program.

“For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.”
While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon.

The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long.

Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

0aab0a15c7086a2d: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely.

eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify.

“Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press.

“The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”
An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming.

It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports, following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237.
No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits.

This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates.

eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones.

“A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.”

Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner.

eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo.

Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business.
The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge.
“Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said. ®

b28b717251c37d86: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web.
The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP.

"Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied."
"We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added.

Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services.

Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns.

PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed.

"The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said.

Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out.
The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations.

The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet.

She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which returns to the Lords on Monday.

"We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector.
AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed, while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®

abfcbfb60201c537: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes.

The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page.

You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them.

“Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.”
From the inside out

Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points.

Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it could be a hacker typing them.”

Given that you can’t run checks on third party organisations, something more sophisticated than regular email security is required. Ideally this would be a GenAI-powered solution that can bring language understanding to bear, able to examine conversation histories in depth to see if something anomalous can be spotted.

It makes life even harder for defenders when the bad actor has successfully assumed the identity of somebody senior. If they are impersonating a top-tier manager with an extensive and trusted reputation then they have a powerful asset on their hands. All the trust and goodwill of that senior individual is now inherited by the criminal.

Conventional email filtering systems will often be configured to allow senior personnel past certain defensive layers with minimal friction, so as not to restrict important business communications. Recipients of mail from such sources may be disinclined to challenge and report them, should suspicions be raised by the nature of what they are asking for. It takes a bold employee to call out as fraud what seems to be a message from somebody at C-level, especially when the email system has apparently green lighted it as authentic.
Bringing the power of AI to bear

The heat is on not just for IT departments but for MSPs who have multiple organisations under their protection, many of which will have no real in-house security knowledge of their own. Kaseya’s own research shows just how exposed many are. New approaches are needed that deal with the menace of account takeover before damage can be caused. And should a takeover transpire, consideration must be given to containing its impact before vital data and infrastructure are affected.

The good news is that modern tools exist that perform just these tasks. INKY is Kaseya's generative AI-driven email analysis tool. It has capabilities that go well beyond any kind of traditional email security, tuned to detect, through the most subtle and marginal signs, when an email conversation is in the process of being infiltrated.

Using techniques such as advanced sender profiling, stylometry and machine learning, INKY is adept at identifying inconsistencies between the known writing patterns of a legitimate employee and the slightly unfamiliar tone of a fake message. It can sniff out that something is wrong, even when message headers seem real, just by spotting the kind of contextual anomalies that expose a phoney message.

INKY is especially useful when it comes to third party account takeover. It achieves this by building and maintaining detailed profiles of trusted senders based on technical and behavioural characteristics. Over time it learns what “normal” looks like and can see when a third-party email doesn’t match a sender’s established profile.
Containing an attack

If a takeover attempt has been successful, there’s more to stemming the damage than just putting a block on a suspect account. By the time of its discovery, a compromised identity may have already led to inroads being made into connected SaaS apps, cloud storage and collaboration tools, widening the possible blast zone well beyond a single email thread.

Modern IT environments are a jungle of identity-driven endpoints and gateways, and therefore increasingly difficult to defend against intruders armed with legitimate credentials. To compound matters, when the bad guys have AI at their disposal they are able to treat these SaaS-driven ecosystems as a single attack surface. Defence that relies on a patchwork of individual tools, each created to solve a particular challenge in one silo of the organisation, will not be up to countering this kind of threat.

That’s why INKY is configured to work with Kaseya SaaS Alerts, a cloud-based detection and response platform designed to help MSPs and others to monitor and protect business applications. Once INKY has picked up that a mailbox has been hijacked, it isolates the user and blocks outbound mail. It then sends an event to SaaS Alerts so that it can lock down that user's access across the rest of the stack. The tools work as a team, INKY blocking the compromised account and SaaS Alerts preventing the damage from spreading.

The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections, user-reported phishing activity and outbound mail protection events. This type of integration helps to automate real-time threat detection across a complex SaaS ecosystem.
“It means if we see suspicious mail going out, we can shut the account down, and take other remedial actions,” says Baggett. “The more you understand the meaning of the mail, the more you can catch.”
Smart tools to the rescue

The battle against account takeover is never won, and future innovation is always needed. We’ve seen how AI is a dangerous weapon in the hands of the attacker. It’s also a very handy tool for the defender – but there are some qualifications: “You can’t just put every inbound and outbound mail through an LLM since the economics don’t add up,” points out Baggett. “You’ve got to be more clever than that.”

One of the most important and cleverest emerging uses for GenAI lies in not simply protecting against account takeover but predicting where weakness might lie, helping to stop a problem before it happens. Baggett believes that the security industry is at the very beginning of being able to use models to predict in this way. An essential preliminary is making sure the many different components that go into securing an organisation can share information with each other.

That integration work is underway, an early example being the real time dialogue between INKY Mail Protection System and SaaS Alerts. Next step is a unified data layer where any security component can publish an event in real time, and any other component can subscribe.

“We’ll continue to make more integrations of this sort over time,” promises Baggett. “We’re also building a centralised capability for AI. With so many of the different components having their own AI, you need an underpinning platform. We also have a service bureau of Machine Learning experts who can make customised models for different tasks. There’s no sleeping on the job. The volume of attacks is clearly going to increase.”
